segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, leaving behind the elementary message about Christ, let us move on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of turning back from dead works and of faith in God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: instruction about washings and the laying on of hands, about the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this we will do, if indeed God permits.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is impossible, when people have once been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift and come to share in the Holy Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: have tasted the goodness of God’s word and the powers of the coming age,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and then have fallen away, to renew them again to turning back, since they are crucifying the Son of God again for themselves and exposing him to public disgrace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For land that drinks the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is farmed, receives a share of blessing from God;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and close to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But about you, dear friends, we are convinced of better things, things that belong to salvation, even though we speak this way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love you showed for his name when you served the holy ones, as you still do.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And we long for each of you to show the same eagerness toward the full assurance of hope right to the end,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you do not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when God made his promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater to swear by, he swore by himself,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “I will surely bless you and surely multiply you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And so, after waiting patiently, Abraham obtained the promise.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For people swear by someone greater than themselves, and an oath given as confirmation puts an end to every dispute among them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when God wanted to show still more clearly to the heirs of the promise that his purpose was unchangeable, he guaranteed it with an oath,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to take hold of the hope set before us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We have this hope as an anchor of the soul, secure and firm, and it enters the inner place behind the curtain,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: where Jesus has entered as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

notes.note: The traditional rendering is 'repentance', which most translations keep as an established term that includes a change of life. In current English 'repent' centres on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction. Here the turn is away from 'dead works' and is paired with faith directed toward God.

Literally 'the word of the beginning of Christ'. The phrase can mean the basic teaching about Christ, as rendered here, or the teaching Christ himself first gave. Most interpreters take it the first way, in line with 'the basic elements' mentioned in 5:12.

The manuscripts differ by one letter. The reading followed here, found in some of the earliest witnesses, makes 'instruction' a description of the foundation itself. Most manuscripts and many editions read 'of instruction', which makes it one more item in the list of what the foundation consists of. The overall sense is little affected.

Many translations have 'baptisms', though several recent ones have 'washings' or 'cleansing rites'. The word is plural and is not the usual New Testament term for Christian baptism; elsewhere it refers to ritual washings (Hebrews 9:10; Mark 7:4). It probably covers teaching that distinguished Christian baptism from other Jewish washings, but exactly what is meant is uncertain.

notes.phrase: crucifying the Son of God again
notes.note: Outside the New Testament this verb regularly means simply 'crucify', with the prefix meaning 'up' rather than 'again'. Early Greek-speaking interpreters and the ancient versions nevertheless understood 'crucify again' here, which suits the context of renewing 'again', and most translations follow them. Some scholars prefer the plain 'crucify'.

The Greek has participles with no conjunction. Most take them as giving the reason ('since they are crucifying'). Some read them as marking time ('while they are crucifying'), which would limit the impossibility to the period in which the rejection continues. The scope of this warning has been debated since antiquity.

Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'. The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue.

notes.phrase: I will surely bless you and surely multiply you.
notes.traditional: Surely blessing I will bless thee, and multiplying I will multiply thee
notes.note: This quotes Genesis 22:17, spoken after Abraham's offering of Isaac, where God introduces the promise with 'By myself I have sworn'. The Greek opens with an oath formula and doubles each verb ('blessing I will bless'), a Hebrew idiom for emphasis that is rendered here by 'surely'.
The two things are generally understood to be God's promise and the oath he added to it. Under Israel's law a matter was established by two witnesses, and here God himself supplies both.

notes.phrase: to take hold of the hope set before us
notes.traditional: to lay hold upon the hope set before us
notes.note: The Greek can be construed in two ways: 'we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to take hold of the hope', or 'we who have fled to take hold of the hope might have strong encouragement'. The verb can also mean 'hold fast' to what one already has. The English word order leaves the first two options open, as the Greek does.

notes.phrase: the inner place behind the curtain
notes.note: The curtain is the one that screened off the innermost room of the tabernacle and temple, the Most Holy Place. Only the high priest entered it, once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). The image prepares for the argument of chapters 7 to 10 that Jesus has entered God's presence itself as high priest.

notes.phrase: according to the order of Melchizedek
notes.note: The wording comes from Psalm 110:4, 'You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek', already quoted in 5:6. Melchizedek is the priest-king of Salem who blessed Abraham in Genesis 14. The author returns here to the theme he broke off at 5:10 and develops it in chapter 7.

candidates.reason: The vocative recurs throughout the letters and translators split between 'beloved', 'dear friends' and 'loved ones'; it needs one choice that reads naturally while keeping the link with love.
The τέλειος word group (mature, perfect, complete) runs through Hebrews, Paul and Matthew, and 'perfection' versus 'maturity' changes the sense considerably.
The noun and its verb range over encouragement, comfort, exhortation and appeal across Acts and the letters, and need sense-by-sense defaults.
'Soul' suggests an immaterial part of a person, where the Greek often means life or self; a consistent policy across the New Testament is needed.
The noun and its verb (v. 15) recur widely and vary in English between patience, longsuffering, forbearance and endurance, and they need to be kept distinct from ὑπομονή.
